Naturalist's Field Reference · Missouri

The Missouri Field Guide

Flora, Fauna & Fungi of the Show-Me State

✓ Edible / Safe ⚠ Caution ⚠ Contact Hazard ✕ Toxic / Poisonous ☠ Deadly ⚡ Venomous

Missouri's diverse biomes — Ozark highlands, floodplain forests, tallgrass prairies, and Bootheel lowlands — support an extraordinary breadth of plant life. This section covers the most significant edible, medicinal, and dangerous plants a person is likely to encounter in the field.

Edible Wild Plants

17 species

American Persimmon

✓ Edible
Diospyros virginiana

Small orange-purple fruit on a common understory tree. Intensely astringent until fully ripe — after first hard frost, turns sweet and rich. One of the best wild fruits in Missouri.

Wait until wrinkled and soft. Premature fruit causes intense mouth puckering. Common statewide on forest edges.

Black Walnut

✓ Edible
Juglans nigra

Missouri's iconic nut tree. Rich, intensely flavored nuts inside a hard shell inside a green-black husk. Husks stain skin and surfaces indelibly. Nuts ripen and fall Sept–Oct.

Wear gloves when processing husks. Allow hulled nuts to cure for 2–3 weeks before cracking. Hulls dye hands brown for weeks.

Cattail

✓ Edible
Typha latifolia

One of the most useful wild plants — nearly every part is edible at some stage. Young spring shoots (like cucumbers), green flower spikes (like corn on the cob), yellow pollen (as flour supplement), and starchy roots year-round.

Found in wetlands, pond margins, and roadside ditches statewide. A forager's staple. The roots can be processed into a flour-like starch.

Dandelion

✓ Edible
Taraxacum officinale

Every part edible — young leaves in salads (bitter, nutritious), flowers in fritters or wine, roots roasted as coffee substitute. Most nutritious wild green available in early spring before leaves turn bitter.

Best collected from unsprayed areas. Young spring leaves (before flowering) are least bitter. Common absolutely everywhere in Missouri.

Elderberry

⚠ Caution
Sambucus canadensis

Clusters of small dark purple-black berries on a large shrub with compound leaves. Found along streams and woodland edges statewide. Berries are edible cooked and used in syrup, wine, and preserves.

Raw berries cause nausea. Leaves, stems, bark, and unripe green berries are toxic — contain cyanogenic glycosides. Always cook the berries. Do not confuse with pokeweed (see Dangerous Plants).

Lamb's Quarters

✓ Edible
Chenopodium album

A common "weed" of gardens and disturbed ground. Young leaves taste similar to spinach and are excellent sautéed or raw. Leaves often have a whitish, mealy coating. Extremely nutritious.

One of the most nutritious wild greens. Best when young and tender. Cook in quantity — wilts dramatically like spinach. Common statewide in disturbed soil.

Pawpaw

✓ Edible
Asimina triloba

Missouri's largest native fruit. Custard-like yellow flesh with a tropical flavor — mango meets banana meets vanilla. Grows in shaded bottomland forest understory, often in patches.

Ripe Aug–Oct. Fruit drops when ready. Does not store well — eat within days. Seeds toxic; do not consume.

Purslane

✓ Edible
Portulaca oleracea

Succulent-leaved sprawling plant found in gardens and disturbed soil. Slightly lemony, mucilaginous texture. High in omega-3 fatty acids — one of the most nutritious wild greens available.

Leaves, stems, and flowers all edible raw or cooked. Slimy texture when cooked works well as a thickener in soups. Common in summer gardens statewide.

Red Mulberry

✓ Edible
Morus rubra

A native tree producing dark red-to-black elongated berries in June. Sweet, slightly tart. Common on forest edges and disturbed areas throughout Missouri. Leaves are highly variable in shape on the same tree.

Fruit stains hands and clothing deeply. Unripe white mulberries can cause mild stomach upset — wait for dark ripeness.

Serviceberry / Juneberry

✓ Edible
Amelanchier arborea

Small tree or shrub blooming white in early spring before most other trees leaf out. Berries ripen in June — purple-red, sweet, with a hint of almond from the seeds. Found throughout Ozark uplands.

One of the first fruits to ripen each year. Birds compete fiercely for them. Excellent fresh, in pies, or dried like raisins.

Shagbark Hickory Nuts

✓ Edible
Carya ovata

Sweet, rich nuts prized by wildlife and foragers alike. Identified by the tree's distinctively shaggy, peeling bark. Thin-shelled compared to other hickories. Found throughout the Ozarks and upland forests.

All Missouri hickory species produce edible nuts. Bitternut hickory (C. cordiformis) is the exception — extremely bitter, though not truly toxic.

Smooth Sumac

✓ Edible
Rhus glabra

Upright shrub with large compound leaves and dense clusters of velvety dark red berries. Common on roadsides, forest edges, and clearings. Berries used to make "sumac-ade" — a tart, lemonade-like drink steeped in water.

Do NOT confuse with Poison Sumac (Toxicodendron vernix), which has white/cream berries in loose clusters and grows in wet, boggy habitats — not roadsides. If berries are red and clustered tightly, it is safe sumac.

Watercress

⚠ Caution
Nasturtium officinale

Peppery aquatic green growing in cool, clear springs and streams. Common in Ozark spring branches. Excellent flavor — use in salads and as garnish.

Harvest only from clean, fast-moving water above any cattle pasture — contaminated water can harbor liver flukes. Ozark spring-fed streams are generally safer sources.

Wild Blackberry & Raspberry

✓ Edible
Rubus allegheniensis / R. idaeus

Thorny cane fruits found along roadsides, forest edges, and clearings. Blackberries ripen June–July; raspberries slightly earlier. Both are excellent eaten fresh, cooked, or preserved.

Ripe berries pull away from the plant easily. No dangerous lookalikes in Missouri when berries are on thorny arching canes.

Wild Garlic / Ramps

✓ Edible
Allium tricoccum / A. canadense

Pungent wild onion relatives. Ramps (wild leeks) appear in early spring in rich moist woods; wild garlic is common in fields and disturbed ground. Leaves, bulbs, and flowers all edible — strong onion/garlic flavor.

CRITICAL: Always confirm the onion smell before eating any wild Allium. Death camas (see Dangerous Plants) can look similar and has NO onion odor. When in doubt, smell the plant.

Wild Strawberry

✓ Edible
Fragaria virginiana

Tiny but intensely flavorful wild version of the cultivated strawberry. Found in open woods, meadows, and roadsides, especially in the Ozarks. Ripens May–June. Five-petaled white flowers precede the fruit.

More flavorful than store-bought varieties despite tiny size. No dangerous lookalikes — the distinctive strawberry flavor and smell confirm identity.

Wood Sorrel

✓ Edible
Oxalis stricta / O. violacea

Clover-like plant with heart-shaped leaflets in groups of three. Bright, lemony-sour flavor from oxalic acid. Pink or yellow flowers. Found in lawns, gardens, and forest understory statewide.

Excellent trail nibble. Contains oxalic acid — harmless in normal quantities, but avoid eating large amounts over extended periods. Do not confuse with true clover.

Dangerous & Poisonous Plants

14 species

Death Camas

☠ Deadly
Anticlea elegans (Zigadenus elegans)

Grass-like leaves arising from a bulb, with creamy-white flowers on a tall spike. Found in open woods, prairies, and glades — especially Ozark glades. Looks similar to wild onion/garlic but has NO onion odor.

Most poisonings occur because it's mistaken for wild onion. Rule: if a plant looks like wild onion but smells like nothing — walk away. All parts are toxic; can be fatal. The smell test is absolute.

Jimsonweed / Datura

☠ Deadly
Datura stramonium

Rank-smelling plant with large white trumpet-shaped flowers and spiny seed pods. Found in disturbed soil, roadsides, and pastures across Missouri. All parts contain tropane alkaloids (atropine, scopolamine, hyoscyamine).

Even skin contact can cause symptoms. Ingestion causes extreme delirium, tachycardia, hyperthermia, and death. Has been used recreationally with fatal results. Do not handle, do not consume any part.

Mayapple

⚠ Caution
Podophyllum peltatum

Large umbrella-like leaves carpet woodland floors in spring. A single white flower blooms under the leaf pair. The yellow egg-shaped fruit, when fully ripe (late summer), is edible and lemon-flavored.

Leaves, roots, stems, and unripe fruit are toxic — contain podophyllotoxin. Only the fully ripe yellow fruit is safe to eat (and only in small amounts). Used in cancer research. Do not eat the seeds.

Moonseed

☠ Deadly
Menispermum canadense

A climbing vine producing clusters of dark blue-black berries resembling wild grapes. Found along forest edges and stream banks across Missouri. The key difference: moonseed has a single crescent-shaped seed; wild grapes have round seeds.

This is one of the most dangerous lookalike situations in Missouri — people die eating these mistaken for grapes. Check: wild grape has tendrils, peeling bark, round seeds and grape smell. Moonseed has none of these.

Nightshade

✕ Toxic
Solanum nigrum / S. dulcamara

Two species common in Missouri. Black nightshade has small white star-shaped flowers and green-to-black berries. Bittersweet nightshade is a climbing vine with purple flowers and red berries. Both are toxic.

Berries are especially dangerous to children who may eat the attractive fruit. Causes nausea, vomiting, and in large quantities, more serious effects. Bittersweet nightshade berries turn from green to orange to red — all stages toxic.

Ohio Buckeye

✕ Toxic
Aesculus glabra

Missouri's native buckeye tree. Produces distinctive round brown nuts with a smooth, shiny patch. The nuts are a classic "lucky charm" carried in pockets — but they are toxic if eaten raw.

Seeds contain aesculin and saponins. Causes vomiting, diarrhea, and neurological symptoms. Historically processed by Native Americans through extended leaching to make flour, but this requires expert preparation.

Poison Hemlock

☠ Deadly
Conium maculatum

The plant that killed Socrates. Biennial herb with hollow purple-spotted stems, fernlike leaves, and flat-topped white flower clusters. Increasingly common in Missouri roadsides, disturbed ground, and stream edges. Smells mousy when crushed.

Causes progressive paralysis. Easily mistaken for wild carrot/Queen Anne's lace or edible umbellifers. Key ID: purple-red blotches on stems, hollow stem, unpleasant smell. Respect this plant.

Poison Ivy

⚠ Contact
Toxicodendron radicans

Missouri's most encountered hazardous plant. "Leaves of three, let it be." Causes intensely itchy, blistering rash from urushiol oil. Can grow as a ground vine, shrub, or massive hairy climbing vine on trees.

Urushiol remains active on dead plants and tools for years. Burning causes severe respiratory distress. All seasons are dangerous — even bare winter stems carry oil. Wash exposed skin immediately with soap and cold water.

Poison Sumac

⚠ Contact
Toxicodendron vernix

A tall shrub or small tree found only in wet, boggy habitats — swamps, bogs, and wet bottomlands. Unlike safe sumacs, poison sumac has white or cream-colored berries in loose clusters, not red berries in tight heads.

Causes rash far more severe than poison ivy — some consider it the most potent urushiol-containing plant in North America. In Missouri, limited mainly to Bootheel swamps and Ozark fens. White berries = danger.

Pokeweed

✕ Toxic
Phytolacca americana

Imposing plant growing 4–10 feet tall with dark purple-black berries in elongated clusters on magenta-pink stems. Found in disturbed areas, forest edges, and roadsides statewide. Birds eat berries without harm — humans cannot.

All parts toxic, especially the root (most dangerous) and berries. Young cooked spring shoots are edible only after multiple boilings with water changes — expert-level foraging only. Avoid. Can be confused with elderberry, which has compound leaves; pokeweed has simple leaves.

Trumpet Creeper

⚠ Contact
Campsis radicans

Common and beautiful native vine with spectacular orange-red tubular flowers, beloved by hummingbirds. Climbs trees, fences, and structures across Missouri. Leaves, stems, and flowers can cause contact dermatitis in sensitive individuals.

Not dangerous for most people, but can cause a mild rash in some. Avoid handling extensively without gloves if you have sensitive skin. Sometimes called "cow-itch vine."

Water Hemlock

☠ Deadly
Cicuta maculata

Considered the most violently toxic plant in North America. Found in wet meadows, stream banks, and marshes statewide. Resembles edible plants like wild parsnip, Queen Anne's lace, and water parsley. Roots are hollow and chambered.

A small piece of root can kill an adult. Causes violent convulsions within minutes. NEVER eat any hollow-stemmed white-flowered plant from a wet area without absolute certainty of identification.

White Snakeroot

☠ Deadly
Ageratina altissima

A common woodland plant with clusters of small white flowers. Historically caused "milk sickness" — the disease that killed Abraham Lincoln's mother Nancy Hanks, contracted from drinking milk from cows that grazed on this plant.

Toxin (tremetol) is passed through milk and meat of animals that eat it. Still found abundantly in Missouri woodlands in late summer and fall. Do not consume any part.

Wild Parsnip

⚠ Contact
Pastinaca sativa

Yellow-flowered plant in the carrot family found along roadsides. The sap causes phototoxic chemical burns — blistering and long-lasting brown scarring when skin contacts sap and is then exposed to sunlight.

Not a rash from allergy — a chemical burn from UV activation. Can cause severe blistering and hyperpigmentation lasting months or years. Wear long sleeves when working near roadside umbellifers in summer.

Missouri is exceptional mushroom country, particularly the Ozarks. The state's oak-hickory forests, abundance of decaying hardwoods, and variable topography create ideal habitat for a remarkable diversity of fungi. The golden rule of foraging: when in doubt, throw it out. Never eat a mushroom unless you are 100% certain of its identity.

Prized Edible Mushrooms

7 species

Chanterelle

✓ Edible
Cantharellus cibarius

Golden-yellow funnel-shaped mushroom with forking false gills (ridges that run down the stem). Found in mixed oak-hickory forest, especially after rain in summer. Fruity, apricot-like aroma.

Can be confused with the toxic Jack-o'-Lantern mushroom. Key difference: chanterelle gills are forking ridges; Jack-o'-Lantern has true, thin, sharp gills. Jack-o'-Lanterns grow in clusters from wood; chanterelles grow singly from soil.

Chicken of the Woods

✓ Edible
Laetiporus sulphureus

Unmistakable bright orange and yellow shelf fungus growing in overlapping fans on living or dead oaks and other hardwoods. Can weigh many pounds. Summer through fall. Tastes remarkably chicken-like when young and tender.

Collect only young, tender outer edges. Older, white-pored sections are too tough. Some people experience GI upset, particularly from specimens growing on locust, conifers, or eucalyptus. Always cook thoroughly.

Giant Puffball

✓ Edible
Calvatia gigantea

White round to oval ball, often soccer-ball sized, found in meadows, fields, and open woods in summer. Edible only when the interior is pure white throughout — once any yellow or purple coloration appears, it is past edibility.

Critical safety check: slice in half and confirm pure white interior with no trace of a developing mushroom outline inside (which would indicate a deadly Amanita button). If all white, it is safe. Never eat a puffball without this check.

Hen of the Woods / Maitake

✓ Edible
Grifola frondosa

Massive clusters of overlapping gray-brown fronds growing at the base of oaks, often the same tree year after year. Fruit bodies can weigh 20+ pounds. Earthy, rich flavor. Found September–November.

One of Missouri's finest culinary mushrooms. Often found at the same tree base year after year — mark your spots. No truly dangerous lookalikes at the base of oaks.

Lion's Mane

✓ Edible
Hericium erinaceus

White, shaggy, icicle-like teeth hanging in a single clump from the wounds of living hardwoods, especially oaks and beeches. Found late summer through fall. Texture and flavor often compared to crab or lobster.

No dangerous lookalikes. The only similar Hericium species are also edible. Collect while pure white — yellowing indicates overripeness and bitter taste. Growing research suggests neurological health benefits.

Morel

✓ Edible
Morchella esculenta / M. angusticeps

Missouri's most celebrated wild mushroom. The honeycomb-pitted cap is unmistakable. Found in spring (April–May) near dying elms, old orchards, cottonwoods, and ash trees. Both yellow and black morels occur in Missouri.

Critical: The cap must be fully attached to the stem and completely hollow when sliced lengthwise. False morels (Gyromitra spp.) have wrinkled caps partially attached to the stem — see Deadly section.

Oyster Mushroom

✓ Edible
Pleurotus ostreatus

White to gray shelf mushrooms growing in clusters on dead hardwoods, particularly cottonwoods and elms. Gills run down a stubby off-center stem. Mild, savory flavor. Found spring and fall, sometimes in winter during warm spells.

One of the most forgiving mushrooms for beginners. The off-center stem, white gills running down it, and growth on dead wood are strong identifiers. Angel wings (Pleurocybella porrigens) look similar but grow on conifers only.

Deadly & Dangerous Mushrooms

6 species

Death Cap

☠ Deadly
Amanita phalloides

Responsible for the majority of fatal mushroom poisonings worldwide. Pale green to yellowish-white cap, white gills, white stem with a ring and a cup-like volva at the base. Found in Missouri associated with oaks. Has a pleasant smell and mild taste.

Half a cap can kill an adult. Symptoms are delayed 6–24 hours — by the time you feel ill, liver and kidney damage is underway. Initial "recovery" after 24 hours is deceptive — organ failure follows. There is no antidote. Learn to identify Amanita species before eating any mushroom from the ground.

Destroying Angel

☠ Deadly
Amanita bisporigera

Pure white from cap to base — gills, stem, and all. Found in oak-hickory forest in summer and fall. Contains the same amatoxins as the death cap. Has been mistaken for button mushrooms, puffballs (when immature), or edible Amanita species.

Same deadly mechanism as death cap. The all-white appearance with a skirted stem and cup at the base are definitive. Rule: any all-white mushroom with gills found in the woods demands expert identification before consideration of eating.

False Morel

☠ Deadly
Gyromitra esculenta

A spring mushroom resembling a morel, with a wrinkled, brain-like or saddle-shaped reddish-brown cap. The cap is irregularly lobed and only partially attached to the stem (not fully attached as in true morels). Interior is chambered, not hollow.

Contains gyromitrin, which converts to the rocket fuel component monomethylhydrazine in the body. Can be fatal. Some people eat it "safely" for years, then suddenly react fatally — individual tolerance varies and worsens with age. The true morel test: slice lengthwise, confirm fully hollow and fully attached.

Fly Agaric

✕ Toxic
Amanita muscaria

Iconic red or orange-red cap with white warts, white gills, and a ringed stem. The classic storybook toadstool. Occasionally found in Missouri. Contains ibotenic acid and muscimol — psychoactive and toxic.

Causes delirium, confusion, vomiting, and in large doses, serious illness. Sought recreationally with dangerous results. Warts wash off in rain — a rainwashed specimen may not show the white dots. An Amanita with a ring and gills warrants extreme caution regardless of color.

Galerina marginata

☠ Deadly
Galerina marginata

Small brown mushroom with a ring on the stem, growing on decaying wood, often in tight clusters. Contains the same deadly amatoxins as the death cap. Frequently mistaken for oyster mushrooms, honey mushrooms, or other edible wood-growers.

The "LBM" (little brown mushroom) killer. This is why experts advise never eating small brown mushrooms without expert verification. Has caused fatalities when collected alongside honey mushrooms by experienced foragers who confused them.

Jack-o'-Lantern

✕ Toxic
Omphalotus olearius

Bright orange mushroom growing in large clusters at the base of oaks or from buried roots. Gills glow faintly in the dark (a unique feature). Frequently mistaken for chanterelles. Causes severe gastrointestinal distress.

Not fatal but causes violent vomiting and diarrhea for many hours. Grows in large clusters from wood (chanterelles grow singly from soil); has sharp, true gills (chanterelles have forked ridges). The clusters and sharp gills are the key differentiators.

Missouri sits at a crossroads of North American wildlife corridors, giving it remarkable mammal, bird, reptile, and aquatic diversity. The Ozark Highlands in particular host species found nowhere else in the Midwest. This section covers the most significant wildlife a visitor or resident will encounter — from excellent table fare to animals that demand respect and distance.

Venomous & Dangerous Animals

10 species

Black Widow Spider

⚡ Venomous
Latrodectus mactans

Shiny black spider with the iconic red hourglass marking on the underside of the abdomen. Females are the dangerous sex; males are tiny and rarely bite. Found under rocks, boards, woodpiles, and in outbuildings across Missouri.

Neurotoxic venom causes severe muscle cramping, pain, and systemic symptoms. Rarely fatal with modern medical care, but bites are a medical emergency. Check under any surface you're about to lift. Wear gloves when handling firewood or moving debris.

Black-Legged (Deer) Tick

⚡ Hazard
Ixodes scapularis

Small tick — nymphs are poppy-seed sized, making them very easy to miss. Primary vector of Lyme disease in the eastern US. Adults are most active in fall (increasing risk in October–November) and early spring. Found in wooded and brushy habitat.

Lyme disease risk in Missouri is real but lower than in the upper Midwest and Northeast. Must be attached 36–48 hours to transmit disease. Daily tick checks after outdoor activity are essential — pay attention to hairline, armpits, groin, and behind knees.

Brown Recluse Spider

⚡ Venomous
Loxosceles reclusa

Missouri is within the core range of this medically significant spider. Tan to brown, 1/4–3/4 inch body, with a violin-shaped darker marking on the back. Found in undisturbed areas: basements, woodpiles, storage boxes, clothing, shoes.

Venom causes necrotic skin lesions in a small percentage of bites — the majority of bites cause only minor reactions. Shake out clothes and shoes left in garages. Check gloves before putting them on. Common in Missouri homes, particularly in older structures.

Copperhead

⚡ Venomous
Agkistrodon contortrix

Missouri's most common venomous snake. Stout body with distinctive hourglass-shaped crossbands in chestnut and copper tones. Found statewide in rocky, wooded terrain, brush piles, and forest edges. Mostly nocturnal in hot weather.

Bites are painful and medically significant but rarely fatal in healthy adults. Bites typically occur when the snake is accidentally stepped on or handled. Give all wide-bodied, patterned snakes a wide berth. Do not reach under rocks, logs, or brush without looking first.

Cottonmouth / Water Moccasin

⚡ Venomous
Agkistrodon piscivorus

Heavy-bodied semi-aquatic pit viper. Adults are dark olive to black; juveniles have copperhead-like banding. Found near water in southern and southeastern Missouri — swamps, sloughs, rivers, and ponds of the Bootheel and Ozark border lowlands. Shows the white interior of its mouth when threatened (the "cotton").

More aggressive than copperheads when cornered. Venom is cytotoxic and can cause severe tissue destruction. Many watersnakes are misidentified as cottonmouths — a non-venomous watersnake will flee; a cottonmouth often holds its ground and gapes. Respect any heavy-bodied, dark waterside snake.

Feral Hog

⚠ Caution
Sus scrofa (invasive)

Invasive and expanding across southern Missouri. Can reach 200–400 pounds. Normally avoids humans, but cornered individuals or sows with young are dangerous. Tusks can cause serious wounds. Highly destructive to habitat.

If you encounter a sounder of hogs, move away calmly. Treeing yourself is a valid option if charged. Aggressive hunting is encouraged — they are a major ecological threat. Report sightings to Missouri Department of Conservation.

Lone Star Tick

⚡ Hazard
Amblyomma americanum

The most common tick in Missouri. Females have a distinctive white dot on their back. Transmits several diseases including ehrlichiosis, tularemia, STARI (Southern tick-associated rash illness), and — critically — can trigger Alpha-Gal Syndrome, causing lifelong red meat allergy.

Alpha-Gal Syndrome is a real and growing concern in Missouri. After sensitization, eating red meat, pork, or lamb can cause severe allergic reactions hours later. One bite can sensitize you permanently. Active April through October statewide.

Snapping Turtle

⚠ Caution
Chelydra serpentina

Large aquatic turtle found in virtually every body of water in Missouri. Can weigh 35+ pounds. On land, they are defensive and will strike with remarkable speed. In water, they are generally docile and avoid humans.

Never handle a large snapping turtle casually — they can reach nearly the length of their shell when striking. The flesh is excellent eating (seven distinct types of meat). Handle by the tail base for transport, keeping the head well away from your body.

Timber Rattlesnake

⚡ Venomous
Crotalus horridus

Missouri's largest venomous snake, reaching 4–5 feet. Heavy-bodied with a distinctive rattle and a dark tail. Found in rocky bluffs, talus slopes, and upland forests — especially Ozark ridges. Dens communally in winter.

Has significant venom quantity. Will rattle as a warning but can strike without rattling if startled. In serious decline due to habitat loss and persecution. Watch your footing on rocky Ozark ledges, especially in warm months. A protected species in Missouri — do not kill.

Western Pygmy Rattlesnake

⚡ Venomous
Sistrurus miliarius streckeri

A small, 18-24 inch rattlesnake with a tiny rattle barely audible beyond a few feet. Grayish with dark blotches. Found in southwestern Missouri, particularly rocky glades and cedar woods. Easy to step on without hearing.

Venom causes significant pain and local tissue damage. The near-inaudible rattle is the major hazard — it cannot warn you at distance like a timber rattler. Wear boots when hiking rocky glade habitat in southwest Missouri.

Edible Wildlife

15 species

Bullfrog

✓ Edible
Lithobates catesbeianus

The largest North American frog. Common in ponds, lakes, and slow streams statewide. Frog legs are a Missouri delicacy — mild, white meat often described as tasting like chicken. Gigging (spearing at night) is the traditional harvest method.

Fishing license and bullfrog permit required for gigging/netting. Pole-and-line fishing for bullfrogs is also legal. Season runs June through October. Gigging at night with a spotlight along pond edges is the classic Missouri experience.

Canada Goose

✓ Edible
Branta canadensis

Abundant in Missouri, particularly along the Missouri and Mississippi flyways and in agricultural areas. Rich, dark breast meat with deep flavor — prepared correctly, one of the finest wild birds. Often unfairly maligned due to poor preparation.

Federal migratory bird hunting stamp plus Missouri waterfowl permit required. Missouri's position on two major flyways makes it a premier destination. Resident geese available in addition to migrating populations.

Crayfish

✓ Edible
Orconectes / Cambarus spp.

Dozens of crayfish species inhabit Missouri's streams — the Ozarks have exceptional diversity, including many endemic species. Common crayfish are excellent boiled in seasoned water and eaten like small crawfish. Excellent protein source from clear Ozark streams.

Missouri has many endemic crayfish species of conservation concern — target only the most abundant common species. Several Ozark species are federally listed as endangered. Identify before harvesting. Used widely as bait and food.

Eastern Cottontail

✓ Edible
Sylvilagus floridanus

Missouri's most abundant small game animal. Found in brushy areas, wood edges, and gardens statewide. Lean, mild white meat similar to chicken. Excellent in stews and braises. Best harvested after the first frost reduces parasite risk.

Wait until after first hard frost — warmer months carry higher tularemia risk (wear gloves when cleaning). An MDC small game permit is required. One of the most important beginner hunting experiences in Missouri.

Gray & Fox Squirrel

✓ Edible
Sciurus carolinensis / S. niger

Both species are excellent table fare, historically a staple of Missouri cuisine. Fox squirrels are larger; gray squirrels are smaller and faster. Gray squirrels prefer dense forest; fox squirrels prefer open woodland and forest edges.

Best in fall when corn and mast crops are available and animals are fat. Squirrel stew with dumplings is a Missouri tradition. Small game permit required. Both species are abundant statewide.

Mallard Duck

✓ Edible
Anas platyrhynchos

Missouri sits on the Mississippi Flyway and attracts extraordinary waterfowl numbers in migration. Mallards, teal, pintails, and dozens of other species stage in Missouri wetlands. Stuttgart to the south may be the duck hunting capital of the world.

Federal duck stamp plus Missouri waterfowl permit required. Mingo National Wildlife Refuge, Fountain Grove Conservation Area, and Swan Lake NWR are legendary waterfowl staging areas. Identification skills are essential for legal and ethical hunting.

Raccoon

✓ Edible
Procyon lotor

Abundant throughout Missouri. Raccoon meat — especially from young animals — has a long tradition in Missouri cooking, particularly in rural areas. Rich, dark meat best prepared slow-cooked or roasted with root vegetables. Historically an important food source.

Trapping and hunting season available with appropriate license. Cook thoroughly to internal temperature of 165°F to eliminate any trichinosis risk, though raccoon is a low-risk species for this parasite in Missouri.

Snapping Turtle (Table)

✓ Edible
Chelydra serpentina

Considered excellent table fare by many Missouri outdoorspeople. Seven distinct muscle types produce varied textures and flavors. Traditionally prepared in snapping turtle soup — a Missouri river-town tradition. Found in virtually every body of water.

Minimum size limit applies in Missouri — check MDC regulations. Handle carefully. Clean promptly. Cook thoroughly. Snapping turtle populations should not be over-harvested — they are slow to reproduce. Turtle soup remains a tradition at some historic Missouri restaurants.

Virginia Opossum

✓ Edible
Didelphis virginiana

North America's only marsupial. Common throughout Missouri. "Possum" has a long culinary tradition in Missouri and the broader South. Fat animals in fall are best. Historically prepared by parboiling then roasting with sweet potatoes.

Highly resistant to rabies due to low body temperature. One of the most ecologically beneficial animals — eats thousands of ticks per season. Consider the population benefit before harvesting. Small game permit required.

White-Tailed Deer

✓ Edible
Odocoileus virginianus

Missouri's most important game animal. Abundant statewide. Lean, flavorful venison is nutritionally excellent. Missouri has one of the highest deer harvests in the nation, with an exceptionally long season.

Requires MDC deer hunting permit. Rifle, archery, and crossbow seasons available. Best venison comes from field-dressing quickly and cooling meat promptly. No chronic wasting disease (CWD) has been detected in Missouri deer as of recent reporting.

Wild Turkey

✓ Edible
Meleagris gallopavo

Missouri has one of the densest wild turkey populations in the country, following remarkable conservation recovery. Found statewide in forest-edge habitat. Spring gobbler and fall season available. Far superior table fare to domestic turkey.

MDC turkey permit required. Spring season targets gobblers; fall season allows both sexes. The breast meat is exceptional; thighs and drumsticks are excellent slow-cooked. Requires patience and woodsmanship to hunt effectively.

Notable Missouri Wildlife

Reference

American Black Bear

Ursus americanus

Rare in SE Missouri Ozarks, expanding from Arkansas. Sightings increasing. Avoid leaving food attractants; no established threat to humans in Missouri.

Bald Eagle

Haliaeetus leucocephalus

Common along Missouri and Mississippi rivers in winter. Missouri is a wintering hotspot. Protected — federally threatened recovery success story.

Bobcat

Lynx rufus

Present statewide in wooded areas. Rarely seen but more common than people realize. No established threat to humans — will avoid contact.

Coyote

Canis latrans

Extremely abundant statewide. Highly adaptable — found from deep wilderness to urban neighborhoods. No season or bag limit in Missouri. No genuine threat to adult humans.

Eastern Bluebird

Sialia sialis

Missouri's state bird. Cavity nester that responded dramatically to nest box programs. Now common in open areas statewide. Brilliant blue males easy to spot along fence lines.

Eastern Box Turtle

Terrapene carolina

Missouri's most commonly encountered turtle on land. High-domed shell with hinged plastron allows it to seal itself completely. Long-lived — individuals can exceed 100 years. Protected in Missouri — do not collect.

Nine-Banded Armadillo

Dasypus novemcinctus

Range expanding northward into Missouri. Now found across the south half of the state. Harmless; roots in soft soil. Historically associated with leprosy — avoid handling.

Ozark Hellbender

Cryptobranchus bishopi

World's largest aquatic salamander, reaching 2+ feet. Critically endangered. Found only in clean, cool Ozark streams. Critically sensitive to water quality. Do not disturb.

Painted Bunting

Passerina ciris

Perhaps North America's most colorful songbird. Males display unmistakable red, blue, and green plumage. Summer resident in SW Missouri. Increasingly uncommon.

Pileated Woodpecker

Dryocopus pileatus

Crow-sized woodpecker with red crest. Found in mature Ozark and Bootheel forests. Rectangular excavations in large dead trees are a sign of their presence. Dramatic bird.

River Otter

Lontra canadensis

Reintroduced and thriving in Missouri rivers. Now found statewide on major waterways. A conservation success. Excellent swimmers, playful behavior.

Wild Boar / Feral Hog

Sus scrofa

Invasive and spreading across southern Missouri. No season restrictions — they may be taken at any time. Report and eliminate on sight to protect native ecosystems.

Missouri lies at the intersection of the eastern deciduous forest, Great Plains, and southern forest regions, creating extraordinary tree diversity. The Ozark Highlands harbor species more typical of the Appalachians; the Bootheel lowlands support bottomland hardwoods of the deep South. Over 150 native tree species call Missouri home.

Oaks (Quercus) — The Dominant Family

Black Oak

Quercus velutina

Common throughout Ozark uplands. Inner bark yields a yellow dye (quercitron). Acorns bitter and tannic — require extensive leaching before use.

Blackjack Oak

Quercus marilandica

Small, scraggly tree of dry, poor soils. Duck-foot shaped leaves unmistakable. Often growing in "post oak barrens" — open, savanna-like habitat.

Bur Oak

Quercus macrocarpa

Missouri's most drought-tolerant oak. Massive acorns with fringed cups. Common on rocky glades and prairie edges. Exceptional lifespan — 400+ years possible.

Chinkapin Oak

Quercus muehlenbergii

Found on rocky, calcareous glades and cliff faces. Distinctive toothed leaves. Produces sweet acorns favored by deer and turkey. Often growing directly from limestone.

Shumard Oak

Quercus shumardii

A large bottomland oak with spectacular fall color. Found in rich lowland soils. One of the largest Missouri oaks — can exceed 100 feet.

White Oak

Quercus alba

The most prized oak. Sweet acorns edible after minimal leaching. Distinctive rounded-lobed leaves. Upland forests statewide. Acorns a critical wildlife mast crop.

Hickories & Walnuts (Juglandaceae)

Bitternut Hickory

Carya cordiformis

Yellow bud scales distinguish it. Extremely bitter nuts — not palatable. Common in moist forests. Important wildlife food despite bitterness.

Black Walnut

Juglans nigra

Missouri's most economically valuable native tree. Rich, distinctive nuts; lumber is extremely valuable. Common in rich, moist soils statewide. Allelopathic — suppresses nearby plants.

Mockernut Hickory

Carya tomentosa

Common throughout Ozarks. Thick-shelled nut; edible but less desirable than shagbark. Fragrant leaves when crushed.

Pecan

Carya illinoinensis

Native to Missouri river bottoms. Wild pecans are small but delicious. Commercial orchards use grafted varieties. Common along Missouri and Osage rivers.

Shagbark Hickory

Carya ovata

Best-eating hickory nut. Peeling, shaggy bark in long gray strips is unmistakable. Upland forests throughout Missouri.

Shellbark Hickory

Carya laciniosa

Similar to shagbark but larger nuts and found in bottomlands. Largest of the native hickory nuts. Good eating.

Maples, Ashes & Elms

American Elm

Ulmus americana

Formerly the great street and riparian tree of the Midwest. Decimated by Dutch elm disease. Some disease-resistant individuals survive along streams. Distinctive asymmetrical leaf base.

Boxelder

Acer negundo

A maple with compound leaves. Very common along streams and disturbed areas. Sap can be tapped for syrup but is of low sugar content. Boxelder bugs associated with this tree.

Silver Maple

Acer saccharinum

Common bottomland tree with silvery leaf undersides. Fast-growing. Often the first tree to flower in late winter. Weaker wood prone to storm damage.

Slippery Elm

Ulmus rubra

Inner bark is slippery and mucilaginous when wet — used medicinally and historically as emergency food. Rougher leaf than American elm. More disease-resistant. Still relatively common.

Sugar Maple

Acer saccharum

Found in the Ozarks and northeastern Missouri. Sap is tappable for maple syrup (requires cold winters). Spectacular fall color — orange to deep red.

White Ash

Fraxinus americana

Once common; now severely impacted by Emerald Ash Borer. Compound leaves with 5–9 leaflets. Many Missouri ashes are dead or dying. A major ecological crisis in Missouri forests.

Distinctive Missouri Trees

Black Cherry

Prunus serotina

Small bitter cherries in long drooping clusters. Fruit edible (jelly, wine) but bitter raw. Wilted leaves are highly toxic — contain prussic acid. Bark and seeds also toxic.

Eastern Red Cedar

Juniperus virginiana

Highly aromatic evergreen. Not a true cedar — a juniper. Blue berry-like cones are edible and used to flavor game and gin. Extremely drought-tolerant; encroaching on native glades statewide.

Eastern Redbud

Cercis canadensis

Oklahoma's state tree. Magenta-pink flowers coat bare branches in early April before leaves emerge. One of Missouri's most beautiful native flowering trees. Flowers edible in salads.

Flowering Dogwood

Cornus florida

Missouri's official state tree. Spectacular white spring flowers (actually bracts). Common Ozark understory tree. Red berries in fall are important bird food — mildly toxic to humans. Threatened by dogwood anthracnose.

Honey Locust

Gleditsia triacanthos

Vicious multi-branched thorns (used as pins historically). Long brown seed pods — pulp edible, sweet. Cultivated thornless varieties common in landscaping.

Kentucky Coffeetree

Gymnocladus dioicus

Large tree with massive compound leaves (largest of any native tree). Seeds were roasted as a coffee substitute by some Native American groups, though raw seeds contain toxic glycoside.

Osage Orange

Maclura pomifera

Produces large chartreuse brain-like fruits ("hedge apples"). Extremely hard, rot-resistant wood historically used for fence posts. Planted widely as living fences. Fruit not edible; seeds edible in quantity.

Pawpaw

Asimina triloba

Small colony-forming understory tree in moist bottomlands. Produces Missouri's largest native fruit. Large tropical-looking leaves. Distinct unpleasant smell when bruised.

Persimmon

Diospyros virginiana

Common forest edge and old field tree. Distinctive blocky, alligator-pattern bark. Outstanding fruit after frost. Dioecious — male and female trees separate.

Sassafras

Sassafras albidum

Three distinct leaf shapes on the same tree (mitten, three-lobed, oval). Root bark makes traditional root beer. Leaves dried and ground are filé powder (Cajun cooking). Aromatic throughout.

Shortleaf Pine

Pinus echinata

Missouri's only native pine. Found in the Ozarks, particularly on dry, rocky ridges in the south. Young shoots and needles can be used to make pine needle tea (high in Vitamin C).

Sycamore

Platanus occidentalis

Missouri's largest native tree by volume. White and tan patchy bark unmistakable. Found along major rivers and streams. Hollow older specimens historically used as shelter.

Quick identification guides for Missouri's most dangerous lookalike situations. A single identification mistake can be fatal in the field. These are the comparisons that matter most.

⚠ Snakebite Protocol

If bitten by a venomous snake in Missouri:

  • Stay calm — anxiety accelerates venom spread. Most Missouri snakebites are not fatal.
  • Remove rings, watches, tight clothing from the bitten limb.
  • Keep the bite below heart level if possible.
  • Call 911 or get to an emergency room immediately. Antivenin is the treatment.
  • Do NOT: cut and suck the wound, apply a tourniquet, apply ice, or use electric shock. These do not help and cause additional harm.
  • Try to photograph the snake if safe — identification helps, but do not delay transport for it.

☠ Mushroom Poisoning

If you suspect mushroom poisoning — even without immediate symptoms:

  • Call Poison Control immediately: 1-800-222-1222
  • Death cap and destroying angel symptoms are delayed 6–24 hours. By the time you feel ill, liver damage has already begun.
  • Save the remaining mushroom or take a photo — identification is critical for treatment.
  • Do not wait for symptoms to worsen. Amatoxin poisoning has a deceptive "recovery" phase followed by liver failure.

Plant Poisoning / Poison Control

Missouri Poison Center: 1-800-222-1222 (24 hours, free)

Call immediately for any suspected plant poisoning — they have experts who can advise on the specific plant and needed response.

True Morel vs. False Morel

✓ True Morel (Safe)

  • Honeycomb pits covering entire cap
  • Cap fully attached to stem at base
  • Completely hollow inside when sliced
  • Cap and stem form one continuous cavity
  • Found near elms, cottonwood, orchards in April–May

✕ False Morel (Deadly)

  • Wrinkled, brain-like, or saddle-shaped cap
  • Cap only partially attached to stem
  • Interior chambered, not fully hollow
  • Cap irregular and lobed, not pitted in neat honeycomb
  • Contains rocket fuel precursor — potentially fatal

Wild Grape vs. Moonseed

✓ Wild Grape (Edible)

  • Forked tendrils opposite leaves
  • Shreddy, peeling bark on vine
  • Round seeds (2–4 per berry)
  • Characteristic grape aroma
  • Berries cluster densely

☠ Moonseed (Deadly)

  • No tendrils — vine wraps around support
  • Smooth stems
  • Single crescent (moon) shaped seed per berry
  • No grape smell
  • Berries resemble small dark grapes

Wild Onion vs. Death Camas

✓ Wild Onion / Garlic (Safe)

  • Strong, unmistakable onion/garlic smell
  • Hollow leaves (in most species)
  • Bulb has onion odor
  • Often purple, pink, or white flowers in umbel

☠ Death Camas (Deadly)

  • NO onion smell — absolutely none
  • Grass-like solid leaves from a bulb
  • Creamy-white flowers on a spike
  • Found on Ozark glades and prairies

The smell test is absolute. If it smells like onion, it is safe. If it looks like onion but has no smell — it is death camas. Do not eat it.

Chanterelle vs. Jack-o'-Lantern

✓ Chanterelle (Edible)

  • Forking ridges (false gills) — blunt, run down stem
  • Grows singly from soil
  • Fruity, apricot aroma
  • Golden yellow, often paler underneath
  • Does not glow in the dark

✕ Jack-o'-Lantern (Toxic)

  • True gills — thin, sharp, knife-blade edges
  • Grows in large clusters from buried wood or root
  • No pleasant aroma
  • Bright orange throughout
  • Gills glow faintly in complete darkness

Identifying Missouri's Venomous Snakes

Missouri has four venomous snake species. Key field identifiers:

  • Copperhead: Hourglass crossbands (narrow on the back, wide on the sides), copper-colored head, unmarked belly. Most commonly encountered.
  • Cottonmouth: Heavy-bodied, dark olive to black adult (juveniles banded). White mouth interior when gaping. Found near water, southern MO.
  • Timber Rattlesnake: Distinctive rattle. Heavy body, dark tail, banded pattern. Rocky bluffs and Ozark ridges.
  • Pygmy Rattlesnake: Small (18–24 in.), tiny almost inaudible rattle. Gray with dark spots. SW Missouri rocky glades.

General rule: Any heavy-bodied, patterned snake warrants caution. Non-venomous watersnakes (Nerodia spp.) are often misidentified as cottonmouths — they will bite defensively but are harmless. Give all snakes space.

Tick Bite Prevention & Removal

  • Wear light-colored clothing to spot ticks easily
  • Tuck pants into socks when in brushy terrain
  • Apply permethrin to clothing (not skin), DEET to exposed skin
  • Do a full-body tick check after any outdoor activity — hairline, behind ears, armpits, groin, behind knees
  • Removal: Use fine-tipped tweezers, grasp tick as close to skin as possible, pull straight upward with steady pressure. Do not twist, burn, or apply petroleum jelly.
  • Save the tick in a sealed bag if possible for identification
  • Monitor the bite site for 30 days; see a doctor if a rash, fever, or flu-like symptoms develop
  • If you develop allergic reactions to red meat weeks or months after a tick bite, ask your doctor about Alpha-Gal Syndrome testing

Safe Foraging Rules for Missouri

  • Positive ID only. Never eat a plant, mushroom, or berry unless you can identify it with complete certainty from multiple characteristics — not just one.
  • The smell test. Any plant resembling wild onion must smell strongly of onion before you consider eating it.
  • White-flowered umbellifers in wet areas (water hemlock / poison hemlock) — treat as deadly unless you have expert-level identification skill.
  • Never eat a mushroom with gills if you're not certain. The most deadly mushrooms (Amanita) are not immediately unpleasant and are easily mistaken for edibles.
  • Berry color is not a reliable safety indicator. Both safe and deadly berries come in red, black, and white in Missouri.
  • When in doubt, don't. No wild food is worth a fatal mistake.

Animal track identification is one of the most valuable wilderness skills in Missouri. The Ozarks, bottomlands, and prairies all support rich wildlife communities. Learn to read the ground — prints, gait patterns, scat, and sign reveal what lives where you walk.

Reading Tracks — The Basics

Gait Patterns

How animals move

Walk/trot: Diagonal pairs (dog, deer). Bound: Hind feet land ahead of fronts (rabbits, squirrels). Lope: Asymmetrical 3-4 print groups (weasels, mink). Packhorse: Hind prints beside front (raccoon). Single-file walking means a relaxed animal; erratic patterns may indicate distress or play.

Track Aging

When were these made?

Fresh tracks have sharp edges and moist soil or compressed snow. Older tracks show crumbled edges, frosted crystal rims, or wind-deposited debris. In mud: exposed tracks dry from outside in. In snow: sublimation can make small prints look large. Compare to your own fresh prints for reference.

Missouri Sign

Beyond tracks

Look for: deer rubs on saplings (velvet shed Aug–Sep; rut scent-marking Oct–Nov), scrapes under overhanging branches (breeding), beaver gnawings (angled cuts, chips), armadillo rooting (circular shallow digs), wild hog wallows (muddy depressions), otter slides on riverbanks, crayfish chimneys near muskrat areas, turkey dust baths in dry sandy soil.

Hoofed Animals

Feral Hog

⚠ Invasive
Sus scrofa

Rounder, blunter toes than deer — less pointed. Dewclaws ALWAYS visible even on hard ground (deer dewclaws only show in soft mud). Wider spread between halves. Often travel in groups (sounders), leaving churned mud.

Rooting sign is unmistakable: large areas of ground completely torn up, as if plowed. Wallows are muddy depressions 3–8 feet across. Boars rub on trees, leaving mud and hair at shoulder height (~3 ft). Report sightings to MDC — they are destructive invasive species.
Tracks & Sign
Scat/Sign: Rooting: large areas of ground completely overturned, 6–12" deep, wider than deer; roots, bulbs, and organic matter scattered. Wallows: muddy depressions, often with hog hair on surrounding bark at shoulder height. Scat: similar to domestic pig but scattered; tubular, 1–1.5" diameter. Rubs: mud and hair on tree trunks 12–24" high. Tracks: cloven like deer but rounder, dewclaws almost always show.

White-tailed Deer

✓ Edible
Odocoileus virginianus

Heart-shaped split hoof, 2–3.5" long. Two pointed halves that register as a V-shape. Dewclaws print behind and to the sides in soft mud or running deer. Walking stride ~18"; running leaps can exceed 15 feet.

Register: hind foot often lands in or near front print when walking (called "perfect register" at slow speed). Running deer leave widely spaced groups of 4. Trails show worn narrow paths in vegetation. Look for rubs on 1–3" diameter saplings (shredded bark Aug–Nov; peak during rut Oct).
Tracks & Sign
Track: Two rounded teardrop-shaped halves forming a heart, pointed at front. Width 2–3.5", length 2–3.5" (bucks larger). Dewclaw impressions show in deep soft substrate or when running — two small round dots behind and above main track. Drag marks between prints in snow (legs lifted less in deep snow). Walking stride: 18–22".
Scat/Sign: Pellets: acorn-shaped, dark brown/black, 0.5–0.75" in clusters of 10–30+. Soft summer scat (green vegetation diet): larger, often clumped or mass. Browse sign: ragged torn twig ends on vegetation 1.5–5 ft high — deer tear, they don't cut cleanly. Rubs: shredded bark on saplings 1–4" diameter at knee-to-shoulder height. Early rubs (Aug–Sep) = velvet removal; peak rubs (Oct–Nov) = rut scent-marking.

Wild Turkey

✓ Edible
Meleagris gallopavo

Three large forward toes + one small rear toe (hallux). Tracks 3.5–4.5" long, splayed. Tracks register alternately in a straddled walk. Toms make longer strides than hens. Drag marks between prints common in winter.

Dusting areas: shallow oval depressions in dry sandy soil with scattered feathers and turkey feces nearby. Scratching sign: parallel scrapes in leaf litter where turkeys rake for food — 12–18" patches. Spring: listen for gobbling at dawn from ridgetops.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Three forward-pointing toes, long and splayed in a Y or K shape. Length 3.5–5" (toms larger). A fourth toe (hallux) may show faintly behind. Stride 6–8", straddle 5–7". Dusting sites: oval hollows 12–18" wide in dry, fine soil near cover edges. Scratch zones: leaves raked back in a crescent pattern exposing bare earth.
Scat/Sign: Classic J-shape or spiral = tom. Bulbous round blob = hen. Both are 0.5–0.75" wide, 1.5–3" long, greenish-brown. Cecal droppings (every ~8th dropping): mustard-yellow, liquid, pungent — normal, not sickness. Feathers at roosting sites under large trees. Primary feathers (10–12") on ground in spring = molting. Strut marks: wing tips drag lines in soft soil in spring.

Canines & Felines

Bobcat

◉ Notable
Lynx rufus

Round print (1.5–2.5"), NO claw marks (retracted claws). 4 round toe pads. Distinctive 3-lobed leading edge on heel pad. Rarely seen but tracks common throughout Missouri. Cat tracks are rounder, dog tracks more oval.

Bobcat scratch posts: vertical scratches 2–3 feet high on tree bark, often near scrapes (bare earth with scat and urine). Stalk-and-pounce hunter — look for crouching impressions in snow near prey. Active dawn/dusk. Track size alone distinguishes from domestic cat (bobcat is significantly larger).
Tracks & Sign
Track: Round, 1.75–2.5", 4 toes arranged in arc with large 3-lobed heel pad. No claw marks (retractile claws). Leading toe offset — two toes on left, two on right of center. Hind steps into front print (direct register) in slow walk — appears as single-print trail. Fur often obscures fine detail. Track size = large house cat but rounder, more symmetrical.
Scat/Sign: Bobcat: 0.5–0.75" wide, segmented with blunt or twisted ends, strong smell, often covered with dirt (cat behavior) or deposited in scrape. Contains hair, bone, feathers. Red fox: Similar to coyote but smaller (0.25–0.5"), often twisted at both ends, placed on prominent spots. Both deposit at territory boundaries. Fox scat has a sharp foxy musk even when dry.

Coyote

◉ Notable
Canis latrans

Oval print, 4 toes with claws (claws always show in canines). 2–2.5" long. Trot gait produces a nearly single-file trail — prints nearly in a straight line. Distinguish from domestic dog: coyote trails are purposeful and straight; dogs meander.

Coyote scat: tapered ends, often contains fur, feathers, berries. Deposited on prominent objects (rocks, stumps) to mark territory. Dens in February–March: look for enlarged burrow openings on south-facing slopes with digging debris outside.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Coyote:2.5" × 2.5", oval, toes and claws close together, prints nearly inline (trot).
Scat/Sign: Twisted rope shape, 0.5–1" diameter, 3–5" long, tapered and often curled at end. May contain: hair, bone fragments, fruit seeds, insects, grass. Deposited on prominent objects (rocks, logs, trail intersections) as territorial marking. Distinctive musky smell. Often gray-tan when dry. Multiple scats at same spot = regular latrine/scent post.

Red Fox

◉ Notable
Vulpes vulpes

Smaller, more elliptical than coyote (1.75–2.25"). Claws show. The red fox produces the most perfectly straight trail of any Missouri canine — hind foot lands precisely in front print. Dense fur between toe pads may cause fuzzy look in winter tracks.

Fox scat looks similar to coyote but smaller. Foxes use latrines (repeatedly scat in same spots). Fox dens often reuse groundhog holes. Pairs mate Jan–Feb; pups emerge April. Gray fox (also common in MO) can climb trees — watch for track trails going up and over brush piles.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Red Fox:2" × 2.5", very oval/elongated, fur between pads may show, neat inline trot trail.

Rodents & Small Mammals

American Beaver

◉ Notable
Castor canadensis

Huge webbed hind print (up to 6"). Small 4-toed front. Wide tail drag mark often obliterates the tracks. Near water — always. Beaver sign is usually more obvious than the tracks: gnawed stumps with pointed tips, dams, lodges, scent mounds.

Gnawed stumps have conical tips and large chip piles at the base. Beaver trees: chips scattered in a "cone" shape around the base. Haul trails from water to timber — packed, muddy, 16–20" wide. Beaver ponds create critical wetland habitat. Missouri populations expanding on most stream systems.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Front: 2.5–3.5", 5 toes with long claws, rounded. Hind: 5–7", large and fan-shaped with full interdigital webbing. Tail drag: a wide flat channel (5–6") between foot prints when walking overland — the most obvious sign. Overland trails from water to feeding trees are well-worn and obvious. Chip mounds of wood fragments surround gnawed stumps.
Scat/Sign: Trees chewed to a conical stump with long vertical tooth grooves (0.25" wide paired incisors). Fresh cuts: pale white wood, chips scattered up to 10 ft. Old cuts: gray/weathered. Prefers: cottonwood, willow, sycamore, box elder (soft hardwoods) but takes others. Bark stripped from fallen branches to transport to food cache (underwater pile near dam). Dams: sticks, mud, bark.

American Black Bear

◉ Notable
Ursus americanus

Front: wide, 5 toes in a curved arc with long curved claws, 4–5". Hind: 7–9", looks remarkably like a large human barefoot print with 5 toes and a distinct heel. Only Missouri mammal with such large humanoid hind tracks.

Rare in Missouri — primarily SE Ozarks (Shannon, Oregon, Reynolds counties), expanding from Arkansas. Report bear sightings to MDC at 573-751-4115. Bear sign: torn-apart logs, turned-over rocks, claw marks 4–6 feet high on smooth-barked trees (territory marking). Do not approach.

Eastern Cottontail

✓ Edible
Sylvilagus floridanus

Classic bound: large hind feet land AHEAD of smaller front feet in a Y-shape or trapezoid. Hind prints 3–4" long; fronts 1–1.5". Four prints per bound group. Hind prints side by side and slightly angled. The go-to Missouri small game animal.

Cottontail form: shallow oval depression in grass or brush where rabbit rests — fur lined, matted grass. Winter browse: look for 45° angle cuts on small twigs and shrubs 6–18" off ground (rabbit reach height). Pellets (scat): small round, golden-green when fresh. Abundant statewide.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Cottontail: 4 toes on round 1.5–2" front prints, 4 toes on larger elongated 3–4.5" hind. Bounding: two large hind prints land side-by-side ahead, two small fronts stagger behind — a Y or exclamation. Squirrel: smaller (front 1", hind 1.5–2"), claws often visible, trail goes tree to tree. Both show bounding pattern; squirrel trails narrower.

Raccoon

✓ Edible
Procyon lotor

The most distinctive Missouri track. Front print: 5 long finger-like toes, ~3". Hind: 5 toes, wider heel, ~4" — looks like a tiny human hand and foot together. Packhorse gait: hind foot beside front foot, printing in pairs.

Raccoon latrines: will repeatedly defecate in the same spot (often the crotch of a tree, a log, or flat surface). Scat is cylindrical, segmented, often contains crayfish shells, berries, corn. Raccoon sign near water: disturbed gravel, overturned rocks searching for crayfish.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Unmistakable hand-shaped prints: 5 long, thin, finger-like toes with long claws splayed widely. Front: 2–3", round. Hind: 3–4.5", elongated like a narrow human foot. Usually found in pairs (front and hind together, "packhorse" gait). Almost always near water. Night animals — fresh tracks in morning mud are common near streams.
Scat/Sign: Raccoons use communal latrines — large accumulations of dark scat on large logs, at base of trees, on flat rocks near water. Tubular, 0.25–0.5" diameter, 2–3", blunt ends. May contain berries (purple-black), crayfish parts, seeds, corn kernels. Caution: raccoon roundworm (Baylisascaris) eggs in scat can be dangerous — do not disturb.

Virginia Opossum

✓ Edible
Didelphis virginiana

Unmistakable hind print: 5 toes with an opposable thumb-like hallux pointing sideways at 90°. Hallux has NO claw. Front has 5 pointed toes. Tail drag line often visible. Waddling gait with 2-print groups offset.

Opossum scat: resembles small dog scat but often contains insect parts. No other Missouri mammal has the sideways-thumb hind track. Very slow walker — rarely seen running. North America's only marsupial; young ride on mother's back in spring.
Tracks & Sign
Track: Distinctive star pattern. Front: 1.5–2", 5 toes with claws splayed at angles. Hind: 2–2.5", hairless opposable thumb (no claw) points sharply to the side — unique to opossum. Tail drag mark often visible between paired prints. Waddling gait. Straddle very wide. Tracks often confused with opossum "handprint" shape near ponds.

Weasel Family & Other Waterway Animals

Muskrat

◉ Notable
Ondatra zibethicus

Small (1–1.5") 5-toed prints with a thin, sinuous tail drag line that snakes between the prints — the signature feature. Partially webbed hind feet. Near water, always. Muskrat sign is often more obvious than tracks: push-ups (mounded vegetation in frozen water) and cattail lodges.

Muskrat push-ups: piles of aquatic vegetation 12–18" across on frozen pond surfaces — feeding stations under the ice. Lodges look like small beaver lodges but made of cattails and reeds. Feeding platforms: cut cattail stems in 6–12" lengths piled on logs at water's edge. Common throughout Missouri wetlands, ponds, and slow streams.

River Otter

◉ Notable
Lontra canadensis

Webbed 5-toed print, 3–4.5". Round with partial webbing showing. Loping gait produces 2×2 print groups. Most distinctive sign: otter slide — a chute-like impression in mud or snow on riverbanks where otters slide repeatedly for what appears to be play.

Otter latrines (spraints): fishy-smelling scat with fish scales, left on prominent rocks or logs at water's edge. Otter resting haul-outs: worn vegetation on banks near water. Reintroduced to Missouri in the 1980s; now thriving on virtually all major river systems. Listen for chirping/whistling calls at dawn.

Striped Skunk

⚠ Avoid
Mephitis mephitis

5 toes on both front and hind. Front claws extremely long (for digging) — often the most distinctive feature: claws can extend 1" beyond toe pads. Hind claws short. Slow, waddling walk. Musk smell often present in area before tracks are found.

Skunk digging: small conical holes in lawns and meadows (hunting grubs) — like golf tee holes scattered across turf. Carry tomato juice or hydrogen peroxide/baking soda solution in field kit. Skunks can carry rabies — a skunk active during daylight acting confused is a high rabies-risk animal. Do not approach.

Other Distinctive Signs

Snapping Turtle

Chelydra serpentina — Water edges

5 clawed toes on each foot (splayed). Tail drag: a single thick groove down the center between the footprints. Sprawling gait — feet print well out to the sides of the body. Nest digging (June): round 4–6" excavation in soft soil, often in sunny spots far from water. Egg shells scattered = predation.

Nine-Banded Armadillo

Dasypus novemcinctus — South MO

4 toes on front, 5 on hind. Distinctive conical digging depressions 3–6" deep and 4–8" wide scattered in a pattern (searching for grubs). Burrow entrances 6–8" diameter, oval, slanting down. Shell drag mark may show between prints. Expanding range northward.

Groundhog (Woodchuck)

Marmota monax — Statewide

4 toes front with long claws, 5 toes hind. Trot gait with 4-print groups. Burrow entrances 10–12" diameter, mound of fresh earth outside main entrance. Secondary "spy holes" with no mound. Hibernates Oct–Feb; fresh digging in March = active. Common in open fields.

American Mink

Neovison vison — Waterways

Small (1.25–1.5") 5-toed prints. Loping 2×2 bound pattern leaving paired groups. Partial webbing between toes. Almost always along streams, rivers, ponds. Scat: twisted, tapered, fishy smell, deposited on rocks or logs at water's edge. Den: under roots or in bank burrow.

Squirrel (Gray/Fox)

Sciurus carolinensis / S. niger

4 toes front (small), 5 toes hind (larger). Bounding: hind prints land side-by-side AHEAD of staggered front prints. Trails often go tree to tree. Sign: middens (piles of nut shell fragments at base of trees), caches (scattered small diggings), cut twigs, mushrooms wedged in branch crotches to dry.

White-tailed Deer Browse & Rubs

Seasonal sign

Browse: ragged torn twigs (deer lack upper incisors) vs. clean 45° rabbit cuts. Scrapes: bare earth oval 18"–3 ft under overhanging branch, October–November (breeding). Rubs: bark shredded from 1–4" diameter saplings at 1–4 ft height. Licking branches: small twigs broken and chewed overhead.

Missouri offers outstanding freshwater fishing across its 17,000 miles of streams, over 100 major lakes, and the Mississippi and Missouri rivers. From trophy-sized channel catfish in the big rivers to smallmouth bass in crystal-clear Ozark streams, the state's aquatic habitats support some of the finest sport fishing in the Midwest.

Missouri Sport Fish4 species

Channel Catfish

✓ Edible
Ictalurus punctatus

Missouri's most popular sport fish. Found in virtually every river, lake, and large pond in the state. Missouri rivers produce trophy-sized channel cats. Excellent white, mild, firm flesh — superb fried or grilled.

Fishing license required. The Missouri and Osage rivers produce large specimens. Also present: flathead catfish (Pylodictis olivaris) — grows to 100+ pounds — and blue catfish (Ictalurus furcatus). All three are outstanding eating.

Crappie

✓ Edible
Pomoxis annularis / P. nigromaculatus

Both white and black crappie are found in Missouri lakes and rivers. Among the best-tasting freshwater fish available — delicate, white, flaky meat prized by anglers. Schooling fish; when you find them, the catching is excellent.

Best in spring during the spawn when they move shallow. Lake of the Ozarks, Truman Lake, and Table Rock Lake are renowned for crappie fishing. No real size minimum in most Missouri waters — check current MDC regulations.

Largemouth Bass

✓ Edible
Micropterus salmoides

Found in ponds, lakes, and slow-moving rivers throughout Missouri. The state's most popular sport fish. Good to excellent eating when cleaned promptly and cooled. Mild, white, flaky meat.

Many anglers practice catch-and-release for bass, particularly larger fish. Smallmouth bass (M. dolomieu) found in Ozark clear streams are widely regarded as superior table fare, with firmer and cleaner-tasting meat.

Ozark Smallmouth Bass

✓ Edible
Micropterus dolomieu

The Ozark Highlands' signature sport fish. Found in the clear, gravel-bottomed spring-fed streams of the Ozarks — the Jacks Fork, Current, Eleven Point, Big Piney, and countless others. A world-class sport fish in a stunning natural setting.

Many streams are under special management regulations. Some are catch-and-release only. The Missouri Ozarks produce some of the finest smallmouth float-fishing in North America. Check MDC regulations carefully by specific stream.
